```{python}
#| include: false

def beta_app(beta, theta):
    """Apparent transverse speed, in units of c, of a blob moving at speed
    beta (units of c) at angle theta (radians) to the line of sight."""
    return beta * np.sin(theta) / (1 - beta * np.cos(theta))
```

Lecture 21 ended with a jet doing quiet work: pushing the hot gas of a galaxy
cluster aside, bubble by bubble, so that it could not cool. This lecture is
about the jet itself. Jets are the fastest large things we know of. They carry
matter away from a black hole at more than $99\%$ of the speed of light, they
stay narrow for thousands of light-years, and when we film them they appear to
break the speed limit of special relativity. They do not break it, and working
out why is a lovely piece of physics that needs nothing more than the finite
speed of light and a right triangle.

## How to read this lecture

**These notes are the reading for this lecture.** Kutner's §19.2, *Radio
galaxies*, is optional; its §19.2.3 derives the same result as
@sec-superluminal by the same route. The lecture builds one argument, and it is
worth holding onto from the start:

::: {.callout-important title="The idea at the center of this lecture"}
**Jets are streams of matter moving at nearly the speed of light, and when one
points close to our line of sight, it chases its own light toward us, so that
it appears to cross the sky faster than light and appears far brighter than the
jet pointing away.**
:::

*What a jet is* introduces jets and shows that the same phenomenon appears
around newborn stars, stellar black holes and supermassive black holes.
*Seeing a jet* explains how radio astronomers combine telescopes across a
continent, or the whole Earth, to resolve a jet's inner parsec. *Measuring a
jet's speed* turns a motion across the sky into a speed, and finds speeds
faster than light. *Apparent superluminal motion* shows why, and how fast the
jet must really be going. *Why we see only one jet* uses lecture 6's Doppler
beaming to explain why the jet pointed away from us is so often invisible.
*Where jets come from* says briefly what is known about how a black hole makes
one.

## What a jet is {#sec-jets}

A **jet** is a narrow stream of matter and energy fired out of the center of an
accreting system, usually in two opposite directions along the rotation axis.
Lecture 20 introduced them as one of the parts of an AGN, and lecture 15 met
one in the binary SS 433. Two properties define them.

**Jets are highly collimated.** A jet can stay narrower than a few degrees over
a length a million times larger than the region that launched it. The jet of
M87 is visible in radio, optical and X-ray light along about $1.5\ \mathrm{kpc}$, and
radio images trace its start to within about a hundred Schwarzschild radii of
the black hole [@walker2018].

**Jets shine by synchrotron radiation**: electrons moving at nearly the speed
of light spiral around magnetic field lines, and radiate as they turn (lectures
13, 14 and 20). Synchrotron light is mostly radio, so jets are mostly seen with
radio telescopes. Only about one AGN in ten has a powerful jet, and those are
the **radio-loud** AGN of lecture 20.

### Jets are seen on many scales

The same shape turns up wherever matter is falling onto something compact and
spinning [@mirabel1999]:

| where | launched by | length | speed |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| young stars | a protostar and its disk | about a parsec | a few hundred $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$: supersonic, not relativistic |
| microquasars | a stellar black hole or neutron star in an X-ray binary (lecture 15) | about a parsec | from $0.26c$ (SS 433) to $\gamma \approx 2$–$3$ |
| radio galaxies and blazars | a supermassive black hole (lectures 18 and 20) | up to a few megaparsecs | $\gamma \approx 10$–$20$ |

: Jets on three scales. The protostellar jets are called Herbig–Haro objects
[@reipurth2001]; the name **microquasar** was coined for X-ray binaries whose
jets look like a quasar's in miniature [@mirabel1994]. {#tbl-scales}

The speeds of the fast jets are given as a **Lorentz factor** $\gamma =
(1 - \beta^2)^{-1/2}$, where $\beta = v/c$ (lecture 3). Close to the speed of
light, $\gamma$ is a far more sensitive measure than $\beta$: a jet with
$\gamma = 10$ has $\beta = 0.995$, and one with $\gamma = 20$ has
$\beta = 0.9987$.

### A jet's power is mostly not light

**A jet's kinetic power, the energy it carries per second in the motion of its
matter, is usually much larger than the power it radiates.** The radiation is
easy to measure and the kinetic power is not. Astronomers find it the way
lecture 21's Perseus example did: a jet ends in a cocoon of hot plasma that
pushes the surrounding gas aside, the work it has done is $pV$ for each
bubble (times a few, for the bubble's own energy), and dividing by the bubble's
age turns that energy into a power. The answer is often ten to a hundred times
what the jet emits as light. Most of what a jet carries is delivered to its
surroundings, which is exactly what made it a candidate for radio-mode feedback.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

1. Find the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ for jets moving at $\beta = 0.9$, $0.99$
   and $0.999$, and then the speed $\beta$ for jets with $\gamma = 2$, $3$,
   $10$ and $20$.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The Lorentz factors are $\gamma = 2.29$, $7.09$ and $22.4$, and the speeds
   are $\beta = 0.866$, $0.943$, $0.995$ and $0.9987$.
   :::

2. M87's jet is about $1.5\ \mathrm{kpc}$ long. How many years does it take a
   blob moving at $\beta = 0.98$ to travel from the black hole to the end of
   it?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About $5000$ years.
   :::

3. Explain why the light a jet emits is a poor guide to how much energy the jet
   is carrying, and why the bubbles it inflates are a better one.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
   Ask what fraction of the energy each one records. The light is only the part
   the jet lost on the way; the bubble records the work done by everything the
   jet delivered at its end.
   :::

:::

## Seeing a jet {#sec-interferometry}

To film a jet moving, we need to resolve its inner parsec, at a distance of
tens or hundreds of megaparsecs. That is far beyond any single telescope.

**A single dish is limited by diffraction.** From lecture 19, the smallest
angle a telescope of diameter $D$ can resolve at wavelength $\lambda$ is

$$
\theta = 1.22\,\frac{\lambda}{D} ,
$$ {#eq-diffraction}

with $\lambda$ and $D$ in the same units and $\theta$ in radians. Radio
wavelengths are long, so radio dishes resolve badly. One of the VLA's
$25\ \mathrm{m}$ dishes, observing at $6\ \mathrm{cm}$, resolves only about
$10$ arcminutes, a third of the width of the full Moon.

**An interferometer combines dishes far apart.** Two dishes separated by a
**baseline** $B$ both record the same incoming wave, and by comparing the two
records it is possible to resolve detail as fine as

$$
\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{B} ,
$$ {#eq-baseline}

as though the two dishes were pieces of one giant dish of diameter $B$. With
many dishes, and many baselines in many directions, a computer can
reconstruct a full image. The collecting area is still only that of the dishes
themselves, so an interferometer sees fine detail but not faint sources.

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: how fine a detail can the VLBA see?"}
**The question.** The Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) is ten $25\ \mathrm{m}$
dishes spread from Hawaii to the Virgin Islands, with a longest baseline of
$8600\ \mathrm{km}$. Observing at $\lambda = 2\ \mathrm{cm}$, what is the
smallest angle it can resolve, in milliarcseconds? And how large is that at the
distance of M87, $16.8\ \mathrm{Mpc}$?

Put the baseline in centimeters first, with a conversion fraction:

$$
B = 8600\ \mathrm{km} \times \frac{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}
  = 8.6 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm} .
$$

Then @eq-baseline, with the units attached:

$$
\theta \approx \frac{2\ \mathrm{cm}}{8.6 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}} .
$$

The centimeters cancel. *Do the units make sense?* An angle in radians is a
pure number, so yes. The numbers give $\theta = 2.3 \times 10^{-9}$ radians.
In milliarcseconds,

$$
2.3 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{rad} \times
  \frac{206265''}{1\ \mathrm{rad}} \times
  \frac{1000\ \mathrm{mas}}{1''} = 0.48\ \mathrm{mas} .
$$

**About half a milliarcsecond**, a hundred times sharper than the Hubble Space
Telescope. A small angle times a distance is a length, so at M87,

$$
2.3 \times 10^{-9} \times 16.8\ \mathrm{Mpc} \times
  \frac{10^{6}\ \mathrm{pc}}{1\ \mathrm{Mpc}} = 0.039\ \mathrm{pc} ,
$$

**about $8000\ \mathrm{AU}$**, or about sixty Schwarzschild radii of M87's
black hole.
:::

**The hard part is timing.** The wave from the source reaches the two dishes at
different times, because one dish is farther from the source than the other. On
a baseline across the Earth the difference can be tens of milliseconds, and it
changes as the Earth turns. To compare the two records, that delay has to be
taken out, by holding one record back by exactly the right amount before
combining them, and it has to be right to a small fraction of a wave period,
a small fraction of a nanosecond for centimeter waves. Dishes that are wired
together, like the VLA's, can share a clock. Dishes on different continents
cannot, so each records its signal with a hydrogen-maser atomic clock, and the
records are combined later at a central computer called a **correlator**. This
is **very long baseline interferometry** (VLBI), and it was VLBI that first
showed jets moving faster than light [@whitney1971].

**Arrays at radio wavelengths** include the VLA in New Mexico (baselines up to
$36\ \mathrm{km}$), the VLBA, and the European and global VLBI networks. **At
millimeter wavelengths**, ALMA in Chile and NOEMA in France are connected arrays,
and the Event Horizon Telescope of lecture 16 is VLBI at $1.3\ \mathrm{mm}$ on
baselines as long as the Earth. <!-- american-spelling: ignore-begin  (official name of the array) -->
The Square Kilometre Array, under construction in
Australia and South Africa, will be the next large one.
<!-- american-spelling: ignore-end -->

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

   $6\ \mathrm{cm}$, in arcminutes, using @eq-diffraction. Then find the
   resolution of the whole VLA at its largest spacing, $36\ \mathrm{km}$, at the
   same wavelength, in arcseconds, using @eq-baseline.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}

   :::

2. The Event Horizon Telescope observes at $1.3\ \mathrm{mm}$ on baselines up to
   the Earth's diameter, $12{,}700\ \mathrm{km}$. What resolution does
   @eq-baseline give, in microarcseconds? Compare it with the size of M87\*'s
   ring, $42\ \mu\text{as}$ (lecture 16).

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About $21\ \mu\text{as}$, half the size of the ring: just enough to see it
   as a ring, and not enough to see much more.
   :::

3. Two VLBA dishes are $8600\ \mathrm{km}$ apart. What is the largest possible
   difference in the time the same wavefront takes to reach them? How far does
   light travel in one nanosecond, and how many $2\ \mathrm{cm}$ waves is that?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   The largest delay is for a source on the horizon, along the line joining the
   two dishes, where the wavefront has to cross the whole baseline. About
   $29\ \mathrm{ms}$; light travels $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ in a nanosecond, which is
   $15$ waves. A timing error of one nanosecond would scramble the comparison
   completely.
   :::

4. How large would a single dish have to be, using @eq-diffraction, to match
   the VLBA's resolution of $0.5\ \mathrm{mas}$ at $2\ \mathrm{cm}$?

:::

## Measuring a jet's speed {#sec-speed}

**A jet is made of knots, or blobs**, that move outward from a bright, fixed
**core** where the jet starts. Image the jet once a year with VLBI, or with the
Hubble Space Telescope for a nearby one, and the blobs move. What is measured
directly is an angle: how far across the sky the blob moves each year, its
**proper motion** $\mathrm{d}\phi/\mathrm{d}t$. (Here $\phi$ is a position on the
sky, to keep $\theta$ free for the next section.) If the galaxy's distance $d$ is
known, from Hubble's law (lecture 18), the small-angle relation turns this into a
speed across the sky:

$$
v_{\mathrm{app}} = d\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} ,
$$ {#eq-vapp}

with $\phi$ in radians. The subscript is for **apparent**, and the reason will
be clear in a moment.

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: a blob that moves one milliarcsecond a year"}
**The question.** A blob in the jet of a radio galaxy $100\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ away
moves $1.0\ \mathrm{mas}$ farther from the core each year. How fast is it moving
across the sky, in units of $c$?

The proper motion in radians per year, with the conversions written out:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} &= 1.0\ \frac{\mathrm{mas}}{\mathrm{yr}} \times
  \frac{1''}{1000\ \mathrm{mas}} \times
  \frac{1\ \mathrm{rad}}{206265''} \\[0.8em]
  &= 4.85 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{rad\,yr^{-1}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Then @eq-vapp, with the distance in centimeters and the year in seconds:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{\mathrm{app}} = {} &
  \left(100\ \mathrm{Mpc} \times \frac{3.086 \times 10^{24}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{Mpc}}\right) \\[0.8em]
  & \times \left(4.85 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}\right)
  \frac{1\ \mathrm{yr}}{3.156 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The megaparsecs cancel in their fraction and the years in theirs, and the radian
is a pure number. *Do the units make sense?* Centimeters per second is a speed, so
yes. The numbers give $v_{\mathrm{app}} = 4.74 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$,
and dividing by $c = 3.00 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$,

$$
\beta_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{v_{\mathrm{app}}}{c} = 1.6 .
$$

**The blob appears to move at $1.6$ times the speed of light.**
:::

Results like this were first found in quasars in 1971 [@whitney1971], and they
are now routine. The MOJAVE program has filmed the jets of hundreds of AGN with
the VLBA for decades, and finds apparent speeds up to about $50c$, with the
most common values between $5c$ and $15c$ [@lister2009]. Jets in our own
Galaxy do it too: the microquasar GRS 1915+105 shot out two blobs in 1994, one
of which appeared to move at $1.25c$ [@mirabel1994].

So either the distances are wrong, or something is moving faster than light, or
the speed in @eq-vapp is not the speed of anything. **The third is right.** The
distances are not the problem, since the galaxies are where Hubble's law puts
them (lecture 18). And no object is moving faster than light.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## Apparent superluminal motion {#sec-superluminal}

The explanation was worked out by Martin Rees in 1966, five years before the
first observation [@rees1966]. It depends only on the fact that light takes
time to reach us.

:::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

Picture a blob moving at nearly the speed of light, aimed close to, but not
exactly at, us. It sends out a flash at point A. Over the next while it moves
to point B, and sends out a second flash. **Because the blob has moved toward
us, the second flash has less distance to travel than the first.** So the two
flashes arrive at our telescope separated by much less time than actually
passed between them.

But we judge the blob's speed by how far it moved across the sky divided by the
time between the two flashes *as we receive them*. The distance across the sky
is real. The time is shortened, by the blob's head start in the race toward us.
Divide a real distance by a shortened time, and the speed comes out too high,
and when the blob is fast enough and the angle is small enough, faster than
light.

**This is not time dilation, and it is not any other effect of relativity.**
The same thing would happen to sound, if a sound source moved toward you at
nearly the speed of sound. Relativity enters in one place only: it is the
reason the blob's real speed must be less than $c$, which is what makes the
apparent speed a puzzle in the first place.

### Mathematical explanation

```{python}
#| label: fig-geometry
#| fig-cap: "The geometry of apparent superluminal motion. A blob moves from A to B at speed $\\beta c$, at an angle $\\theta$ to the line of sight; the observer is far below the figure. In a time $\\Delta t$, it moves $\\beta c\\,\\Delta t\\,\\sin\\theta$ across the sky and $\\beta c\\,\\Delta t\\,\\cos\\theta$ toward the observer, which is the head start that shortens the time between the two flashes."
#| fig-alt: "A diagram with a vertical dashed line labeled line of sight, running downward to an arrow labeled to the observer. A point A sits at the top of the line. A solid arrow runs from A downward and to the right to a point B, labeled beta c delta t, at an angle theta to the vertical. A horizontal dotted segment from the vertical line to B is labeled beta c delta t sine theta, the motion across the sky. A vertical dotted segment along the line of sight from A down to the level of B is labeled beta c delta t cosine theta, the motion toward the observer."
#| fig-height: 3.6

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 3.6))
th = np.radians(25)
L = 1.0
A = np.array([0.0, 1.0])
B = A + L * np.array([np.sin(th), -np.cos(th)])
ax.plot([0, 0], [1.08, -0.45], ls="--", color=MUTED, lw=1)
ax.annotate("", xy=(0, -0.55), xytext=(0, -0.3),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK2, lw=1.2))
ax.text(0.03, -0.56, "to the observer", color=INK2, fontsize=10, va="center")
ax.text(-0.04, -0.12, "line of sight", color=MUTED, fontsize=10,
        rotation=90, ha="right", va="center")
ax.annotate("", xy=B, xytext=A,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=BLUE, lw=2))
ax.plot(*A, "o", color=INK, ms=6, zorder=3)
ax.plot(*B, "o", color=INK, ms=6, zorder=3)
ax.text(A[0] + 0.03, A[1] + 0.04, "A", fontsize=12)
ax.text(B[0] + 0.03, B[1] - 0.02, "B", fontsize=12)
ax.plot([0, B[0]], [B[1], B[1]], ls=":", color=ORANGE, lw=1.6)
ax.text(B[0] / 2, B[1] - 0.07, r"$\beta c\,\Delta t\,\sin\theta$",
        color=ORANGE, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11)
ax.plot([0.012, 0.012], [A[1], B[1]], ls=":", color=AQUA, lw=2.2)
ax.text(-0.06, (A[1] + B[1]) / 2 - 0.15, r"$\beta c\,\Delta t\,\cos\theta$",
        color=AQUA, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=11)
ax.text(*(A + 0.55 * (B - A) + np.array([0.06, 0.03])), r"$\beta c\,\Delta t$",
        color=BLUE, fontsize=11)
arc = np.linspace(-np.pi / 2, -np.pi / 2 + th, 30)
ax.plot(0.22 * np.cos(arc), A[1] + 0.22 * np.sin(arc), color=INK2, lw=1)
ax.text(0.075, A[1] - 0.36, r"$\theta$", fontsize=11, ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(-0.75, 0.75)
ax.set_ylim(-0.65, 1.15)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
```

**Set up the geometry** of @fig-geometry. A blob moves at speed $v = \beta c$
in a direction making an angle $\theta$ with our line of sight, with
$\theta = 0$ straight at us. It emits a flash at A, and a time $\Delta t$ later,
by the blob's own reckoning in the galaxy, emits another at B. In that time it
has moved $\beta c\,\Delta t$, which splits into two pieces:

* across the sky, $\beta c\,\Delta t \sin\theta$;
* toward us, $\beta c\,\Delta t \cos\theta$.

**The flash from B has less distance to travel**, by $\beta c\,\Delta t
\cos\theta$, so it saves a time $\beta\,\Delta t \cos\theta$. The two flashes
therefore arrive separated by

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{obs}} = \Delta t - \beta\,\Delta t\cos\theta
  = \Delta t\,(1 - \beta\cos\theta) .
$$ {#eq-tobs}

**The apparent speed** is the distance across the sky divided by the time we
measure:

$$
v_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{\beta c\,\Delta t \sin\theta}{\Delta t\,(1 - \beta\cos\theta)} ,
$$

and dividing by $c$,

$$
\beta_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{\beta\sin\theta}{1 - \beta\cos\theta} .
$$ {#eq-betaapp}

*Do the units make sense?* Both sides are speeds divided by $c$, pure numbers,
so yes. For a slow blob, $\beta \ll 1$, the denominator is $1$ and
$\beta_{\mathrm{app}} = \beta\sin\theta$, the ordinary projected speed. The
denominator is what makes the difference: as $\beta \to 1$ and
$\theta \to 0$, it goes to zero.

**The fastest it can appear.** For a given $\beta$, which angle gives the
largest $\beta_{\mathrm{app}}$? Differentiate @eq-betaapp with respect to
$\theta$ and set the result to zero:

$$
\frac{\beta\cos\theta\,(1 - \beta\cos\theta) - \beta\sin\theta\,(\beta\sin\theta)}
     {(1 - \beta\cos\theta)^2} = 0 .
$$

The denominator cannot vanish, so the top must. Dividing it by $\beta$,

$$
\cos\theta - \beta\left(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\right) = 0 ,
$$

and since $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$,

$$
\cos\theta = \beta .
$$

Then $\sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - \beta^2} = 1/\gamma$, and putting both into
@eq-betaapp,

$$
\beta_{\mathrm{app,max}} = \frac{\beta/\gamma}{1 - \beta^2} = \beta\gamma .
$$ {#eq-betamax}

So a jet with $\gamma = 10$ can appear to move at up to about $10c$, and the
fastest apparent speeds tell us the smallest Lorentz factors the jets can have.

**The slowest jet that can appear superluminal.** Setting
$\beta\gamma = 1$ gives $\beta^2 = 1 - \beta^2$, or

$$
\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71 .
$$ {#eq-betamin}

**Below about $0.71c$, no angle makes a jet appear faster than light.** Above
it, some range of angles always does.

**Going backward.** What we measure is $\beta_{\mathrm{app}}$, and we want
$\beta$. Solving @eq-betaapp for $\beta$,

$$
\beta = \frac{\beta_{\mathrm{app}}}{\sin\theta + \beta_{\mathrm{app}}\cos\theta} .
$$ {#eq-betainv}

This needs the angle, which is rarely known. But @eq-betamax gives a floor
without it: since $\beta_{\mathrm{app}} \le \beta\gamma$, the real speed must
satisfy $\beta\gamma \ge \beta_{\mathrm{app}}$, which is
$\gamma \ge \sqrt{1 + \beta_{\mathrm{app}}^2}$.

### Numerical exploration

@fig-bapp plots @eq-betaapp for four speeds, in the style of the slide from
lecture. Each curve rises to a peak at $\cos\theta = \beta$, and the peak is
$\beta\gamma$. The faster the jet, the taller and narrower its peak, and the
closer to the line of sight it sits.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bapp
#| fig-cap: "Apparent speed across the sky, $\\beta_{\\mathrm{app}}$, against the angle $\\theta$ between the jet and the line of sight, for jets with real speeds $\\beta = 0.5$, $0.8$, $0.95$ and $0.99$ (@eq-betaapp). The dotted line marks the speed of light; any part of a curve above it is apparent superluminal motion. Each dot is the curve's maximum, $\\beta\\gamma$, at $\\cos\\theta = \\beta$."
#| fig-alt: "A chart of apparent speed, from 0 to 8, against angle to the line of sight, from 0 to 90 degrees. Four curves start at zero at zero degrees and rise to a peak before falling. The curve for beta 0.5, gray, stays well below 1 everywhere, peaking near 0.58 at 60 degrees. The curve for beta 0.8, aqua, peaks just above 1, at 1.33 near 37 degrees. The curve for beta 0.95, orange, peaks at about 3 near 18 degrees. The curve for beta 0.99, blue, rises steeply to a peak of about 7 at 8 degrees and then falls, dropping below 2 by about 55 degrees. A horizontal dotted line at 1 marks the speed of light. All four curves end at the real speed beta at 90 degrees."
#| fig-height: 4.0

betas = [0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 0.99]
colors = [INK2, AQUA, ORANGE, BLUE]
theta_deg = np.linspace(0.05, 90, 900)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.0))
for i, b in enumerate(betas):
    col = colors[i % len(colors)]
    ax.plot(theta_deg, beta_app(b, np.radians(theta_deg)), color=col, lw=2,
            label=rf"$\beta = {b}$")
    g = 1 / np.sqrt(1 - b**2)
    ax.plot(np.degrees(np.arccos(b)), b * g, "o", color=col, ms=6, zorder=3)
    print(f"beta = {b}: peak {b * g:.2f} at {np.degrees(np.arccos(b)):.1f} deg")
ax.axhline(1, color=MUTED, ls=":", lw=1.2)
ax.text(42, 0.92, "speed of light", color=MUTED, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(0, 90)
ax.set_ylim(0, 8)
ax.set_xticks([0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90])
ax.set_xlabel(r"angle to the line of sight $\theta$ (degrees)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"apparent speed $\beta_{\mathrm{app}}$")
ax.legend(fontsize=10, loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

INK2, AQUA, ORANGE, BLUE, MUTED = "#52514e", "#1baf7a", "#eb6834", "#2a78d6", "#898781"

betas = [0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 0.99]     # real speeds, in units of c  # <- edit this


def beta_app(beta, theta):
    """Apparent transverse speed, in units of c, of a blob moving at speed
    beta (units of c) at angle theta (radians) to the line of sight."""
    return beta * np.sin(theta) / (1 - beta * np.cos(theta))


colors = [INK2, AQUA, ORANGE, BLUE]
theta_deg = np.linspace(0.05, 90, 900)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.0))
for i, b in enumerate(betas):
    col = colors[i % len(colors)]
    ax.plot(theta_deg, beta_app(b, np.radians(theta_deg)), color=col, lw=2,
            label=rf"$\beta = {b}$")
    g = 1 / np.sqrt(1 - b**2)
    ax.plot(np.degrees(np.arccos(b)), b * g, "o", color=col, ms=6, zorder=3)
    print(f"beta = {b}: peak {b * g:.2f} at {np.degrees(np.arccos(b)):.1f} deg")
ax.axhline(1, color=MUTED, ls=":", lw=1.2)
ax.text(42, 0.92, "speed of light", color=MUTED, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(0, 90)
ax.set_ylim(0, 8)
ax.set_xticks([0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90])
ax.set_xlabel(r"angle to the line of sight $\theta$ (degrees)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"apparent speed $\beta_{\mathrm{app}}$")
ax.legend(fontsize=10, loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

:::

::::

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: a jet at 0.99c, ten degrees from the line of sight"}
**The question.** A blob moves at $\beta = 0.99$, at $\theta = 10^{\circ}$ to
our line of sight. For every year that passes in the galaxy, how much time
passes between the flashes we receive, and how fast does the blob appear to
move across the sky?

Start with @eq-tobs, for $\Delta t = 1\ \mathrm{yr}$:

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{obs}} = \left(1\ \mathrm{yr}\right)
  \left(1 - 0.99 \cos 10^{\circ}\right) .
$$

*Do the units make sense?* The bracket is a pure number, so the answer is in
years, a time, so yes. Since $\cos 10^{\circ} = 0.9848$, the bracket is
$1 - 0.9750 = 0.0250$, and

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{obs}} = 0.025\ \mathrm{yr} ,
$$

**about nine days.** A year of the blob's travel reaches us compressed into nine
days. In that year, it moved across the sky by $\beta\sin\theta =
0.99 \times 0.1736 = 0.172$ light-years. So, by @eq-betaapp,

$$
\beta_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{0.172\ \mathrm{ly}}{0.0250\ \mathrm{yr}} = 6.9\ \mathrm{ly\,yr^{-1}} .
$$

A light-year per year is the speed of light, so the units are already a
multiple of $c$.

**About seven times the speed of light**, from a blob that is moving at less
than it. By @eq-betamax, the most this blob could appear to move is
$\beta\gamma = 0.99 \times 7.09 = 7.0$, at $\theta = 8.1^{\circ}$, so ten
degrees is close to the best angle.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .textbook-watch title="Textbook watch: is it a relativistic effect?"}
Kutner's §19.2.3 introduces this explanation as *"an alternative explanation,
involving a special relativistic effect."* The derivation that follows uses no
relativity at all: no time dilation, no length contraction, only the time light
takes to travel. That is the right physics; the label is not. Relativity's only
role is to forbid $\beta > 1$, which is why the effect needs explaining. Kutner's
derivation itself, his equations 19.4 to 19.8, is the same as the one above.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## Why we see only one jet {#sec-boosting}

Jets come in pairs, fired out of both poles. Yet in the images, most jets are
one-sided: a bright jet on one side of the core, and on the other side, faint
emission or nothing at all. The explanation is lecture 6's **Doppler beaming**.

Lecture 6 defined the **Doppler factor**
$\mathcal{D} = 1/[(1 + v_r/c)\,\gamma]$, where $v_r$ is the velocity away from
us, and showed that a moving source's brightness scales as $\mathcal{D}^4$.
For a jet at angle $\theta$, the radial velocity is $v_r = -\beta c\cos\theta$
for the approaching jet and $+\beta c\cos\theta$ for the receding one, so

$$
\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{1}{\gamma\,(1 - \beta\cos\theta)} ,
\qquad
\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rec}} = \frac{1}{\gamma\,(1 + \beta\cos\theta)} .
$$

The approaching jet carries the same factor $1 - \beta\cos\theta$ that made it
appear superluminal. The two jets are identical except for their direction, so
the ratio of their brightnesses is

$$
\frac{F_{\mathrm{app}}}{F_{\mathrm{rec}}}
  = \left(\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{app}}}{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rec}}}\right)^{4}
  = \left(\frac{1 + \beta\cos\theta}{1 - \beta\cos\theta}\right)^{4} ,
$$ {#eq-jetratio}

and the factors of $\gamma$ cancel, as they did for the disk in lecture 6.
The power of 4 is for a single blob, as in lecture 6. A steady, continuous jet,
and a real synchrotron spectrum, give a somewhat smaller power, closer to 2 or
3 [@urry1995], but the conclusion below does not change.

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: how much fainter is the counterjet?"}
**The question.** Two identical jets move at $\beta = 0.98$, at
$\theta = 20^{\circ}$ to the line of sight. How many times brighter does the
approaching jet appear than the receding one?

Here $\beta\cos\theta = 0.98 \times 0.9397 = 0.9209$, so @eq-jetratio gives

$$
\frac{F_{\mathrm{app}}}{F_{\mathrm{rec}}}
  = \left(\frac{1.9209}{0.0791}\right)^{4} = (24.3)^{4} .
$$

*Do the units make sense?* A ratio of two fluxes is a pure number, and so is
everything on the right, so yes. The answer is

$$
\frac{F_{\mathrm{app}}}{F_{\mathrm{rec}}} = 3.5 \times 10^{5} .
$$

**About a third of a million.** With a power of 2 instead of 4 it would still
be about $600$. Either way, an image good enough to show the approaching jet
clearly is nowhere near good enough to show the other.
:::

@fig-boost shows @eq-jetratio against angle. For a jet across our line of sight,
$\theta = 90^{\circ}$, the two sides are equally bright; within a few tens of
degrees of the line of sight, the counterjet vanishes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-boost
#| fig-cap: "The brightness of the approaching jet relative to the receding one, against the angle $\\theta$ between the jet and the line of sight, from @eq-jetratio, for real speeds $\\beta = 0.5$, $0.9$ and $0.99$. The vertical axis is logarithmic: each labeled step is a factor of a hundred. Only jets lying nearly across the sky show two sides of similar brightness."
#| fig-alt: "A chart with a logarithmic vertical axis, from 1 to 10 to the tenth, against angle to the line of sight from 0 to 90 degrees. Three curves fall from left to right and all meet at a ratio of 1 at 90 degrees. The curve for beta 0.5, gray, starts near 80 at zero degrees. The curve for beta 0.9, aqua, starts near 10 to the fifth. The curve for beta 0.99, blue, starts above 10 to the ninth and is still above 10 to the fourth at 30 degrees."
#| fig-height: 3.8

betas_b = [0.5, 0.9, 0.99]
colors_b = [INK2, AQUA, BLUE]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.8))
for b, col in zip(betas_b, colors_b):
    bc = b * np.cos(np.radians(theta_deg))
    ax.plot(theta_deg, ((1 + bc) / (1 - bc)) ** 4, color=col, lw=2,
            label=rf"$\beta = {b}$")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0, 90)
ax.set_ylim(0.8, 1e10)
ax.set_yticks([1, 1e2, 1e4, 1e6, 1e8, 1e10])
ax.minorticks_off()
ax.set_xticks([0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90])
ax.set_xlabel(r"angle to the line of sight $\theta$ (degrees)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$F_{\mathrm{app}} / F_{\mathrm{rec}}$")
ax.legend(fontsize=10, loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

**Beaming also selects what we find.** A jet pointed nearly at us is not only
faster on the sky, it is far brighter, by a factor of $\mathcal{D}^4$ over what
it would be at rest, and $\mathcal{D}$ can be $20$ or more. So the brightest
jets in the radio sky are, out of all proportion, the ones that happen to point
at us. These are the **blazars** of lecture 20, the type 1 view taken to its
extreme: AGN seen straight down the jet, whose light is dominated by the jet
and flickers on a timescale of days, compressed by the same factor
$1 - \beta\cos\theta$. A sample chosen for brightness is a sample of jets
aimed at the Earth, which is why so many of MOJAVE's jets are superluminal.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## Where jets come from {#sec-launch}

How a black hole makes a jet is not completely settled, but the outline is
agreed: **jets are made by magnetic fields, wound up by rotation** [@blandford2019].

Gas in an accretion disk carries magnetic field with it (lecture 16). Where
that field reaches the inner disk and the black hole, rotation twists the field
lines into a tight spiral along the spin axis, like a coiled spring, and the
spring pushes plasma outward along the axis and squeezes it into a narrow beam.
There are two places the energy can come from.

* **The disk.** Field lines anchored in the rotating disk fling gas outward
  along them, like beads on a spinning wire [@blandfordpayne1982].
* **The black hole's spin.** Field lines that thread the horizon of a spinning
  black hole are dragged around by the spacetime itself, in the ergosphere of
  lecture 2, and that extracts the black hole's rotational energy
  [@blandford1977]. This is the **Blandford–Znajek process**.

Computer simulations of disks full of magnetic field around rapidly spinning
black holes find jets whose power exceeds $\dot{M} c^2$, the whole rest-mass
energy of the gas being accreted, which is only possible because the energy is
coming from the spin [@tchekhovskoy2011]. That would make the efficiency of
lecture 7, for the jet alone, larger than one. Whether real jets are powered
this way is one of the things the Event Horizon Telescope's images of M87 are
being used to test.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## If you want to go further

None of this section is needed for what comes before or after.

**Kutner, §19.2.** The chapter 19 PDF in Canvas Files describes radio galaxies,
their lobes and jets, and in §19.2.3 derives apparent superluminal motion, with
the image of the quasar 3C 279's jet from @wehrle2001.

**The MOJAVE movies.** The MOJAVE program [@lister2009] has posted animations of
its VLBA images, one per jet, on its website at Purdue University. They show
the blobs moving.

**The reviews.** Begelman, Blandford and Rees [-@begelman1984] is the classic
account of how radio sources work; Blandford, Meier and Readhead
[-@blandford2019] is the modern one.

## Summary

| idea | result | why it matters |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Jets | narrow, two-sided, synchrotron-emitting streams | found around young stars, stellar black holes and supermassive ones |
| Jet speeds | $\gamma \approx 10$–$20$ for AGN | the fastest large things known |
| Jet power | kinetic power is many times the radiated power | jets can heat their surroundings |
| Interferometry | $\theta \approx \lambda/B$ | VLBI resolves a fraction of a milliarcsecond |
| Proper motion | $v_{\mathrm{app}} = d\,\mathrm{d}\phi/\mathrm{d}t$ | blobs appear to move faster than light |
| Superluminal motion | $\beta_{\mathrm{app}} = \beta\sin\theta/(1 - \beta\cos\theta)$ | light-travel time, not new physics |
| Maximum apparent speed | $\beta\gamma$, at $\cos\theta = \beta$ | a floor on the Lorentz factor |
| Slowest superluminal jet | $\beta = 1/\sqrt{2}$ | below it, no angle works |
| One-sided jets | $F_{\mathrm{app}}/F_{\mathrm{rec}} = [(1 + \beta\cos\theta)/(1 - \beta\cos\theta)]^4$ | the counterjet is lost; blazars are jets aimed at us |
| Launching | magnetic fields wound up by the disk or the spin | a jet can tap the black hole's rotational energy |

A jet that appears to move faster than light is a jet moving at nearly the speed
of light toward us, chasing its own light. Everything that made it look fast,
the head start on its light, also makes it look bright, and makes the jet that
points away from us all but invisible. That leaves one question about black
holes that this course has not yet touched: what happens at the horizon when
quantum mechanics is taken into account. Next time, black holes get a
temperature.
